strategy.title: No plan inside the $1,500 capital ceiling: Fraser fir loads need $6,300 paid at pickup
strategy.why: The only opening (three signed $9,000 trailer-load purchases, payable on delivery) requires paying Blue Ridge Fir Farms $6,300 in full at pickup before any buyer pays, so one load ties up $6,300 against a $1,500 capital ceiling. Every other chain link is established; capital alone rules every plan out.

alternatives.title: Sell one $9,000 load with capital raised to $6,300
alternatives.why: One load settles $9,000 in about 6 days, more than the $5,000 target, if the owner allows $6,300 of capital.

alternatives.title: Negotiate a buyer deposit or supplier credit
alternatives.why: No record shows a buyer deposit or supplier credit term; the supplier quote says payment in full at pickup, so this is not established.

To make it supportable, capital: allow the goal to commit at least $6,300, what the lots that reach the target need at once; or target: lower the target: the openings held bring nothing inside the goal's limits even with every buyer agreeing. The conclusion covers the openings held; markets nobody has counted are not ruled out, so Brain keeps searching for openings outside them.

facts.value: Sell Wholesale Fraser fir trailer loads for nonprofit fundraiser tree lots to each buyer.
Blue Ridge Fir Farms (quoted $6,300 a load, payment in full at pickup) quoted to do the work.
Volunteer organisers of church and school Christmas tree fundraiser lots
Three fundraiser-lot organisers signed to buy a 300-tree trailer load at $9,000, payable on delivery (signed purchase agreements, 2026-11-20).

reviews.reasons: NO_PLAN is correct and its decisive gap is a genuine constraint. The single opening has every link established: three signed purchase agreements at $9,000 per 300-tree load payable on delivery, a named fulfiller (Blue Ridge Fir Farms, $6,300 a load, payment in full at pickup), 6 days to cash against 25. But the supplier must be paid $6,300 before any buyer pays, so the minimum exposure of any plan using it is $6,300 = 4.2x the $1,500 ceiling; even with all the evidence in hand no schedule fits the limit, and no deposit or supplier-credit term is on the record (assuming one would read an unknown as favourable). The constraint is cited to the card's exposure and directCosts fields. Brain independently reaches the same verdict (INFEASIBLE AS STATED, capital >= $6,300). The resolution is right. One precision for the owner: one load collects $9,000 but keeps $2,700 after the $6,300 supplier payment; if the owner counts only cash beyond what they advanced, two loads run back to back (load 2 funded from load 1's day-6 receipts, peak still $6,300) keep $5,400, still inside 25 days.
findings: INFO cop_ac2c276adb63453bbdb7 ECONOMICS: peak funding $6,300 at pickup vs $1,500 exposure cap — binding CAPITAL constraint.
LOW: resolution should state that one load nets $2,700 after supplier cost; two sequential loads (peak $6,300) net $5,400 if net cash is what the owner means.
